extracted.intended_audience: California Air Resources Board (CARB), EPA staff, engine/vehicle manufacturers, environmental and administrative law practitioners, and other stakeholders in CAA section 209 waiver/authorization proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate a State request (California) for authorization under Clean Air Act §209(e) to adopt/enforce nonroad engine emission standards, including within-the-scope determinations for amendments. The page explains the statutory criteria, evidentiary burdens, procedural steps, and related analytical subcriteria EPA uses in making authorization decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization criterion — protectiveness determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The Administrator will grant the authorization if California determines that its standards will be, in the aggregate, at least as protective of public health and welfare as otherwise applicable federal standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CARB must make a protectiveness determination (e.g., Res. 08-42, Res.10-48). EPA's review is limited to whether California's determination was arbitrary and capricious; EPA presumes California's determination satisfies the requirement absent clear evidence to the contrary. For within-the-scope confirmations, amended regulations must not undermine the original protectiveness determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization criterion — not arbitrary and capricious
rubrics_metrics.description: The authorization will not be granted if the Administrator finds that California's determination is arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents bear the burden of proving that California's determination is arbitrary and capricious. EPA must make a reasonable evaluation of the record and may set aside a decision if it ignores material evidence or relies on unsupported assumptions. Lack of adverse comment or contrary evidence supports finding that the determination is not arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization criterion — need to meet compelling and extraordinary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The authorization will not be granted if the Administrator finds that California does not need such standards to meet compelling and extraordinary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inquiry is limited to whether California needs its own mobile-source pollution program to address compelling and extraordinary conditions (e.g., geographic/climatic conditions and concentration of vehicles). EPA historically accepts California's showing unless commenters present evidence that California no longer needs a separate program. Within-the-scope confirmations generally do not require re-analysis under this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization criterion — consistency with section 209 (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The authorization will not be granted if California's standards and accompanying enforcement procedures are not consistent with section 209 of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluates consistency by reference to section 209(a), section 209(e)(1), and section 209(b)(1)(C) (as applied via section 202(a)). The scope of EPA's review is narrow and circumscribed to statutory questions; EPA gives substantial deference to California's policy judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with section 209(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be consistent with section 209(a), California's nonroad standards and enforcement procedures must not apply to new motor vehicles or new motor vehicle engines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA checks whether the California regulation expressly applies only to off-road/nonroad vehicles and does not reach motor vehicles as defined in the Act. If the regulation is limited to nonroad engines, it meets this consistency check absent contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with section 209(e)(1) (preempted categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be consistent with section 209(e)(1), California's standards and enforcement procedures must not attempt to regulate engine categories permanently preempted from state regulation (e.g., new farming or construction vehicles/engines below 175 hp, new locomotives or their engines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA verifies that the California standards do not affect these preempted categories. CARB's representations that the rules do not affect such categories are relevant; lack of contrary comment supports consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with section 209(b)(1)(C) / section 202(a) — technological feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: California standards are inconsistent with section 202(a) if there is inadequate lead time to permit the development of necessary technology, giving appropriate consideration to the cost of compliance within that time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA assesses whether adequate technology exists or whether there is adequate time to develop and apply requisite technology and whether the cost of doing so is feasible. Past waivers and decisions inform the analysis. Opponents bear the burden of showing technological infeasibility; absence of such evidence supports authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with section 209(b)(1)(C) / section 202(a) — certification and test procedure consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: California's accompanying enforcement procedures would be inconsistent with section 202(a) if California test procedures impose certification requirements inconsistent with federal test procedures, making it impossible for manufacturers to meet both using the same test vehicle or engine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA compares federal and California testing/certification procedures for conflicts. If California has not modified test procedures since prior waivers and the amendments include no new test procedures, EPA typically finds no inconsistency. Commenters must identify specific conflicts to defeat authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Within-the-scope determination criteria for amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to previously authorized California regulations may be confirmed 'within-the-scope' (without full authorization review) if: (1) the amended regulations do not undermine California's previous determination that its standards are, in the aggregate, at least as protective as federal standards; (2) the amended regulations do not affect consistency with section 209; and (3) the amended regulations do not raise any 'new issues' affecting prior authorizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If all three conditions are met, EPA may grant a within-the-scope confirmation. CARB must show the amendments meet these criteria; EPA will consider comments challenging any of the three conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: New issues inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will determine whether amendments raise any 'new issues' affecting prior authorizations; if they do, a within-the-scope confirmation may be inappropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CARB should identify whether amendments create new, more stringent requirements or force any change in technology; absence of new issues (and no adverse comment) supports a within-the-scope finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and standards of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents of a waiver/authorization bear the burden of showing that the statutory criteria for denial have been met; the Administrator must make a reasonable evaluation of the record. The standard of proof varies with the finding involved (e.g., 'clear and compelling evidence' required to show enforcement procedures undermine protectiveness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedents (e.g., MEMA I) establish that California's submissions are presumed to satisfy the requirements and that those opposing must persuade the Administrator otherwise. EPA applies a reasonableness standard in evaluating evidence; failure of opponents to meet their burden supports authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to California and limited scope of EPA review
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA gives substantial deference to California's policy judgments and limits its inquiry to the specific authorization criteria identified in section 209(e)(2)(A); EPA does not second-guess broader policy choices (e.g., cost-benefit balancing) if the statutory criteria are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical and legislative context supports a narrow EPA review. Arguments not specified in the statute (for example, that a requirement is an unwise regulatory choice) are not legally pertinent to the authorization decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory consideration of safety factors for small engines (<50 hp)
rubrics_metrics.description: In considering requests to authorize standards for new nonroad spark-ignition engines smaller than 50 horsepower, the Administrator will give appropriate consideration to safety factors (including potential increased risk of burn or fire) associated with compliance with the California standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety concerns specific to small engines should be raised and supported with evidence; EPA must consider such safety factors when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative/procedural requirements — public notice, comment, hearing, and docketing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA provides notice of receipt of California's authorization request, invites public comment, provides an opportunity to request a public hearing, and maintains a public docket containing documents relied upon in making the decision (available via regulations.gov and EPA reading rooms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of written comments or hearing requests may result in EPA not holding a hearing and proceeding on the written record. Parties should submit evidence into the public docket to affect EPA's determination. The public docket excludes confidential business information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final action effects and judicial review timing
rubrics_metrics.description: A final authorization action may be designated as of national applicability and scope; judicial review of such final actions is available only in specified courts (here, U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) and within statutory deadlines (e.g., petitions for review must be filed by a specified date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders must file petitions for review in the correct court and by the stated deadline (e.g., petitions for review must be filed by February 8, 2016 for this action), and cannot obtain judicial review in subsequent enforcement proceedings under section 307(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of record/evidence considered — materiality and relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's consideration of evidence is circumscribed to that which is relevant to the statutory questions under section 209(e)(2)(A); evidence must pass a threshold test of materiality to be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments outside the statutory criteria (e.g., marginal air quality improvements not commensurate with costs) are not legally pertinent. Parties should present material evidence directly bearing on protectiveness, need, or consistency criteria to influence the decision.
